cardiac in origin because of the diﬀ use spread of pain into these 
other areas. For many patients, pain is worse at night when they 
are lying down. Complications of untreated or unresponsive 
GERD may include impaired swallowing, aspiration of gastric 
contents into the lungs, ulceration, and perforation or stricture
of the esophagus. Barrett’s esophagus is also considered to be a
complication of GERD (see “Barrett’s Esophagus—A Complica-
tion of GERD”).
Treatment for GERD includes three major goals: (1) increasing
LES competence; (2) decreasing gastric acidity, and thus de-
creasing the severity of symptoms; and (3) improving clearance
